title: Layer a Graph Into the Most Levels
statement:
You get an undirected graph with n nodes, numbered 0 to n − 1, and a list of edges. The graph may be disconnected.

Assign every node to a level numbered 1, 2, …, m so that every level is used and, for every edge, the two ends sit on levels that differ by exactly 1. Think of laying out a diagram where each connection goes one row up or down, never sideways and never skipping a row.

Return the largest possible m, or -1 if no valid assignment exists.

examples.why: Levels 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→4 and 4→1. Node 4 cannot get its own level because it must sit right next to node 1's level.
Going around the triangle changes the level three times by ±1, which cannot bring you back to where you started.
The square fits in 3 levels (0, then 1 and 3, then 2). The separate pair 4–5 gets 2 more levels of its own.

hints: When is it impossible? Walk around a cycle: each edge moves you one level up or down.
A cycle of odd length can never return to its starting level, so the graph must be bipartite. Each connected component is independent, so the answer is a sum over components.

Inside one component, BFS from a start node puts every node on level 1 + its distance. That is valid, and the number of levels is 1 + the largest distance. Try every node as the start and keep the best per component.

explain.intuition:
Each edge changes the level by exactly one, so going around any cycle changes the level an odd number of times if the cycle is odd, and you cannot get back to the start. An odd cycle means -1; no odd cycle means the component is bipartite, and then layering works.

For a bipartite component, BFS from any node s gives a valid layering: put each node on level 1 + dist(s, node). Every edge joins two nodes whose distances differ by exactly one (by at most one in any BFS, and never zero in a bipartite graph). Can you beat the best BFS? No: in any valid layering, take a node s on the top level; a node on level L is at distance at least L − 1 from s, so the level count is at most the BFS depth from s. So the best layering of a component is the largest BFS depth over all starting nodes, and components simply add up.
steps: Build an adjacency list and label connected components.
For every node s, run BFS. If an edge ever joins two nodes at the same distance, the component has an odd cycle: return -1.
Otherwise the BFS uses 1 + max distance levels; keep the maximum per component.
Return the sum of the per-component maxima.
pitfalls: Running BFS only from one node per component. The farthest-reaching start can be any node; in a path you must start at an end.
Taking the maximum over the whole graph instead of summing per component. Separate components stack their levels independently.
Forgetting isolated nodes. Each one is its own component and adds one level.

solutions.title: All-pairs distances
solutions.idea: Two-colour each component to rule out odd cycles, compute all distances with Floyd–Warshall, and add 1 + the largest distance inside each component.

solutions.title: BFS from every node
solutions.idea: A BFS from each node both detects odd cycles (an edge inside one BFS layer) and measures how many layers that start gives. Keep the best per component and add them up.

followups: n grows to 10⁵ but the graph is a forest. How do you get each tree's best layering in linear time?
Return an actual level assignment, not just the count.
